parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about the job of the core as a magnetic path - iron is magnetised far more easily than air, so where do you want almost all the magnetic field lines from the primary coil to go?
parts.proper_answer: The iron core confines and guides the magnetic flux from the primary coil to the secondary coil, reducing loss of magnetic flux to the surroundings.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Flux Has To Get From Primary To Secondary**
You can picture the primary coil creating magnetic field lines when current flows in it. For the transformer to work well, as many of those lines as possible must pass through the secondary coil. That is what we mean by good flux linkage.

Step 2: **Why Iron Is Better Than Air**
Air is a very poor magnetic path and lets flux spread out and leak away. Iron has high permeability, so it acts like an easy motorway for magnetic flux. It concentrates the flux and carries it round the loop of the core straight through the secondary coil, so very little is lost.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Remember the solid iron core is itself a conductor sitting in a changing magnetic field - what does electromagnetic induction produce inside the iron itself?
Hint 2: Think about how slicing the core into thin insulated sheets changes the size of the loops that current can flow around, and what smaller current means for heating by $I^2R$.
parts.proper_answer: Lamination breaks up the core and increases its resistance to circulating currents. This reduces the size of eddy currents induced in the core, so heating of the core and wasted power are reduced.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **The Core Suffers Induction Too**
The changing flux does not only link the coils, it also passes through the conducting iron core. By Faraday's law a changing flux induces an e.m.f. in any conductor, so small circulating currents called eddy currents are induced in the iron itself.

Step 2: **Eddy Currents Waste Energy As Heat**
Those eddy currents flow through the resistance of the iron and dissipate power as heat. That is wasted energy that lowers the efficiency of the transformer and can overheat it.

Step 3: **How Laminations Help**
Laminating means building the core from thin sheets of iron insulated from each other instead of one solid block. The insulation breaks up the large loops, forcing eddy currents into much smaller paths with higher resistance. Smaller eddy currents mean much less heating.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Start from what the secondary coil needs in order to have an e.m.f. - does Faraday's law require just magnetic flux, or a changing magnetic flux?
Hint 2: Work back to the primary coil - compare the magnetic field produced by an alternating current with that produced by a steady constant direct current.
Hint 3: Follow the chain from primary to core to secondary to see what happens to the output if the core flux stops changing after switch-on.
parts.proper_answer: An alternating input voltage produces an alternating current and hence a continuously changing magnetic flux in the core. This changing flux links the secondary coil and, by Faraday's law, induces a continuously alternating e.m.f. in the secondary. A constant voltage would produce a steady flux with no change, so no e.m.f. would be induced.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Induction Needs Change**
A transformer works by electromagnetic induction. An e.m.f. is induced in the secondary only when the magnetic flux linking it is changing. No change in flux means no induced e.m.f. That is the heart of Faraday's law.

Step 2: **Alternating Input Gives Changing Flux**
With an a.c. input, the primary current keeps reversing direction. So the magnetic field it creates keeps reversing too, producing a continuously changing flux in the iron core.

Step 3: **Changing Flux Links To The Secondary**
The core carries that changing flux to the secondary coil, so the flux linkage of the secondary keeps changing. This induces an alternating e.m.f. at the output with the same frequency as the input.

Step 4: **Why Constant Voltage Fails**
With a constant d.c. input, after a very brief moment at switch-on the primary current and the core flux become steady. The rate of change of flux is then zero, so Faraday's law gives zero induced e.m.f. in the secondary. That is why a transformer cannot work continuously on d.c.
